newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia polling stations open doors, voting begins.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia polling stations open doors, voting begins.

text.p: Polling stations opened across Bosnia on Saturday as the country prepared to vote in its first post-war election, set by last year's Dayton peace accord to try to heal the wounds of war and usher in a democratic future.
Witnesses said most of the 4,600 polling stations across the war-ravaged country appeared to open on time at 7 a.m. (0500 GMT). Early voting was light, with no incidents reported.
Hundreds of thousands of Bosnia's refugees and displaced people were expected to travel along rough roads back to the hometowns they fled during the war to cast their ballots.

Serb refugees arrived in Bosnia through the night, brought by train from Belgrade to vote in the Bosnian Serb Republic. They were shepherded through the dark onto buses to be taken to polling stations.

At one polling station in central Sarajevo, seven elderly people were waiting outside as its doors swung open. The first couple to vote said they were refugees from Pale -- the Bosnian Serb stronghold a short drive from Saraejevo.
Bosnian state radio reported that other polling stations across the country had opened on schedule. It proceeded to give citizens instructions on how to vote.

Some 2.9 million Moslems, Croats and Serbs will elect a national presidency and parliament, a president and separate parliament for the Serb Republic, and a parliament and cantonal administrations in the Moslem-Croat Federation.

At a bus depot in Sarajevo, four refugees sat anxiously waiting to be driven back to their old home districts to vote, the first time they have returned since they were driven out by the ethnic cleansing which marked the 3-1/2 war.
The biggest short-term fear of the international community was of violence between ethnic rivals meeting one another on Saturday in places they once fought over.

To make sure the mass movement of people passes off peacefully, the OSCE and the NATO-led peacekeeping force have drawn up an elaborate security plan that directs voters along 19 "secure" routes across the ethnic boundary lines.

The United States has led a chorus of senior Western officials in publicly proclaiming the country has no choice but to go through with the elections, however flawed, if it is ever to recover from the 43-month conflict.
